citations.quote:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about
forces and motion, in the spacetime, frames and worldlines of
[[post-cm01-spacetime]], [[post-cm01-frames]] and [[post-cm01-worldlines]].

**(i) Setting and configuration domain.** A model of the framework has
$N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed positive masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]], clause (v)) and a configuration domain $Q$ in one
fixed inertial frame, in the unconstrained branch of
[[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a): $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open,
possibly with the collision set $\Delta$ removed when the force law of the
model is singular at coincident positions. The constrained branch of that
definition, with its reaction forces, is **not** covered by this postulate; the
dynamics of constrained systems is a separate development with its own
assumptions. A **state** of the model is a pair $z=(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb
R^{3N}$ of positions and coordinate velocities of the labels in the chosen
frame ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]).

**(ii) Time window.** A model carries a nondegenerate open interval
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, its **time window**, read in seconds
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(iii) Force map and standing regularity.** A **force map** on this data is a
map

$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v)=\bigl(F_{1}(t,x,v),\dots,F_{N}(t,x,v)\bigr),$$

with components of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
([[def-cm01-units]]). The standing hypotheses of this branch, which every
force map of a model is required to satisfy, are:

1. **Continuity.** $F$ is continuous on its domain
   $D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
2. **State-local Lipschitz regularity, locally uniform in time.** $F$ is
   locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z=(x,v)$, locally uniformly in
   time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]: every
   compact cylinder $C\subseteq D$ carries a finite $L\ge0$ with
   $\lVert F(t,z)-F(t,z')\rVert_{2}\le L\lVert z-z'\rVert_{2}$ whenever
   $(t,z),(t,z')\in C$ share their time coordinate.

A map that fails clause 1 or clause 2 is **not** a force map of this branch,
whatever its other merits. When a later statement differentiates the force map
(for instance in a linearization or a smooth-dependence claim), it adds the
required differentiability hypothesis of the state variable explicitly; clause
2 alone licenses only the existence, uniqueness and continuation statements
proved on this page.

**(iv) Equation of motion.** Adopt: the motion of the labels of a model with
force map $F$ in an inertial frame is governed by

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N),$$

imposed along families of $C^{2}$ coordinate curves of the labels
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):J\to Q$, where $J\subseteq I_{0}$ is an interval with
nonempty interior and the derivatives are those of
[[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. The precise notion of a motion of the
model, its associated first-order system and its maximal motions is
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. The force map is **primitive data** of the model:
the equations above are the model's law, not an operational definition of $F$
from a measured acceleration, and $F$ is not an extra observable measured
independently of the motion. The mass $m_{i}$ in (iv) is the fixed inertial
mass of clause (v) of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; no other mass occurs in this
clause.

**(v) Additive composition of force contributions.** When a model presents its
force map as composed of contributions, the composition is the pointwise sum:
for force maps $F^{(1)},\dots,F^{(k)}$ on a common domain satisfying (iii),

$$F(t,z)=\sum_{a=1}^{k}F^{(a)}(t,z),$$

and the sum again satisfies (iii), because a finite sum of continuous maps is
continuous and a finite sum of maps that are locally Lipschitz in the state
variable is locally Lipschitz with a locally uniform constant. This
**superposition of forces** is an adopted modelling rule, not a theorem about
nature: it says how the model's total force is composed from the contributions
it declares. Two decompositions with the same sum define the same force map
and the same model; the framework does not measure an individual contribution
in isolation, and no observation of motions alone determines a decomposition.
Nor does (v) assert that sums of motions are motions: if $F$ is not affine in
the state, the sum of two solutions of (iv) generally does not satisfy (iv),
and superposing solutions is a separate question from superposing forces.

**(vi) Description in another inertial frame.** Let $F_{*}=\bigl(o',u',
(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')\bigr)$ be a second inertial frame related to the frame
of (i) by the Galilean transformation

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x_i'=Rx_i+\upsilon t+a_{0}\quad(i=1,\dots,N)$$

with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a_{0},\upsilon\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$
([[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]] clause 1;
[[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]); $\upsilon$ is the boost velocity
denoted by $v$ in that theorem. Define the block-diagonal map
$$R_{N}:=\operatorname{diag}(R,\dots,R):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$$
and the repeated tuples $\bar a_{0}:=(a_{0},\dots,a_{0})$ and
$\bar\upsilon:=(\upsilon,\dots,\upsilon)$ in $(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$. Thus
$R_N x=(Rx_{1},\dots,Rx_{N})$, and the same componentwise rule applies to
velocities and forces; since $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3}$,
$R_N^{\mathsf T}R_N=I_{3N}$. If $x:J\to Q$ is a family of motions of the
labels in the first frame, then the description of the same worldlines in the second
frame is
$$\eta(t'):=R_{N}x(t'-b)+\bar\upsilon(t'-b)+\bar a_{0}\qquad(t'\in J+b).$$
By clause 2 of the cited theorem, each $\eta_i$ is $C^{2}$ and
$\eta_i''(t')=R\ddot x_i(t'-b)$, so along the motion
$$m_i\eta_i''(t')=R F_i\bigl(t'-b,x(t'-b),\dot x(t'-b)\bigr).$$

Adopt: the same interaction, read in the second frame, is represented on the
transferred data by the force map below. Let $P$ be the inverse affine
transfer from new-frame data to old-frame data,
$$P(t',y,w):=\bigl(t'-b,\,R_N^{\mathsf T}(y-\bar\upsilon(t'-b)-\bar a_{0}),\,R_N^{\mathsf T}(w-\bar\upsilon)\bigr).$$
Its preimage of the original domain is
$$D_{*}:=P^{-1}(D)=\{(t',y,w):P(t',y,w)\in D\};$$
it is open because $P$ is a homeomorphism and $D$ is open. Define
$$F_{*}:D_{*}\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad F_{*}(t',y,w):=R_N F\Bigl(t'-b,\ R_N^{\mathsf T}\bigl(y-\bar\upsilon(t'-b)-\bar a_{0}\bigr),\ R_N^{\mathsf T}(w-\bar\upsilon)\Bigr).$$
The map $F_{*}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in its state variable:
the transfer and its inverse are affine, and at fixed time they act linearly
on state differences; on compact time intervals their state Lipschitz
constants are uniform, so precomposition preserves the stated regularity of
$F$. The framework
formulates the equation of motion in every inertial frame; a rule that does
not transform by this law is a description tied to the frame in which it was
written, and the framework attaches no kinematic covariance to it. When
$Q=\mathbb R^{3N}$ — the case of the models of the companion page — the
transferred domain is again a product
$I_{0}'\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $I_{0}'=I_{0}+b$, and
$F_{*}$ is a force map in the sense of (iii); for a proper open $Q$ the
transferred position set $R_NQ+\bar\upsilon(t'-b)+\bar a_0$ may depend on
$t'$, and the equation is then read on that transferred set.

**(vii) What this branch excludes.** Impulsive forcing (a finite momentum
transfer at an instant is not a force map); Coulomb sliding friction, whose
expression contains the factor $v/\lvert v\rvert$ and is undefined at $v=0$;
static friction, which requires an inequality or a set-valued reaction model;
stochastic forcing; and forces that exist only as distributions. Each of these
requires its own stated model and solution notion, and none is covered by
(iii)–(iv). A singular force law is admissible on a configuration domain with
the singular configurations removed — for instance an inverse-square law on
the collision-excluded $Q$ of clause (i) — and what the removal of those
configurations implies for existence in time is stated by the continuation
theorem of this page.

**(viii) Status.** Clause (iii) states the hypotheses under which the theorems
of this page are proved; clause (iv) is the adopted law of motion; clauses (v)
and (vi) are the adopted composition and frame rules. Nothing here is deduced
from experiment, from a symmetry principle or from the uniqueness theory of
differential equations, and nothing here asserts that any physical
interaction is exactly of this form: the theorems of this page are conditional
consequences of the adopted model. The empirical significance of a concrete
model lies in fully specified model parameters and reported observations
compared with its predictions, and this postulate supplies neither.

**(i) Setting.** Work in the force branch of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with one labeled particle of fixed mass
$m>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)) in a fixed inertial frame, with
time window $\mathbb R$ and configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R^{3}$, and with
the particle's coordinate position $x$ and coordinate velocity
$v=\dot x$ ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]). The particle moves through a
**medium** that fills the region of the motion and is at rest in the chosen
frame. The medium is not one of the model's particle labels, so its effect on
the label is an **external force** of the model in the sense of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]]: the decomposition into the label's own dynamics
and the medium's effect is part of the model's declaration.

**(ii) The model.** Adopt as a **constitutive model** of the medium's net
force the **linear drag model** with a declared coefficient
$c\ge0$ of dimension $\mu\tau^{-1}$, read in kilograms per second
([[def-cm01-units]]):

$$F^{\mathrm{drag}}(v):=-c\,v,$$

optionally combined, through the additive composition of clause (v) of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], with a declared constant applied force
$m\mathbf g$, where $\mathbf g\in\mathbb R^{3}$ is a constant parameter of
dimension $\ell\tau^{-2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The resulting force map of the
model is

$$F(t,x,v)=m\mathbf g-c\,v,\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad m\,\ddot x=m\mathbf g-c\,\dot x,$$

the equation of a label whose only interactions are the constant applied field
and the linear resistance of the medium. The model is defined for all
$(t,x,v)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R^{3}$.

**(iii) Regularity.** The force map is affine in the state: it is continuous;
and for two states $z=(x,v)$, $z'=(x,v')$ sharing a position,
$\lVert F(t,z)-F(t,z')\rVert_{2}=c\,\lVert v-v'\rVert_{2}\le c\,\lVert z-z'\rVert_{2}$,
so it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable with the global constant $c$,
uniformly in time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). It is
therefore a force map of the branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause
(iii), and the existence, uniqueness and continuation theorems of this page
apply to it; the regularity check is recorded with the model checks on the
companion page.

**(iv) Physical status and regime.** This is a **phenomenological**
constitutive model, adopted rather than derived: it represents the net effect
of a medium whose microscopic state is not modelled, and the coefficient $c$
is a model parameter that depends on the body and the medium. The linear form
is a restricted regime — slow motion through a viscous medium, of which the
Stokes force on a sphere, $c=6\pi\eta a$ for dynamic viscosity $\eta$ and
radius $a$, is the recorded example — and other regimes are **different
models**: a force growing quadratically in the speed at higher speeds, or
Coulomb sliding friction, whose expression contains the factor
$v/\lvert v\rvert$ and is undefined at $v=0$, and which is outside clause
(iii) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] altogether. The model also neglects
the random component of the environment's force. The cited fluctuation
qualification is specifically Likharev's damped harmonic oscillator model
$m\ddot q+\gamma\dot q+\kappa q=0$, with $m,\kappa>0$ and damping coefficient
$\gamma>0$ (denoted $\eta$ in the source), oscillator energy
$E:=\tfrac12m\dot q^{2}+\tfrac12\kappa q^{2}$, and natural angular frequency
$\omega_{0}:=\sqrt{\kappa/m}$: footnote 4 says
that neglecting its random-force component is admissible only when, at thermal
equilibrium, $E$ is much greater than $\max(k_{\mathrm B}T,\hbar\omega_{0}/2)$,
where $T$ is temperature, $k_{\mathrm B}$ is Boltzmann's constant and $\hbar$
is the reduced Planck constant. The free-particle model stated here has no
restoring term and defines no corresponding $E$, $T$ or $\omega_{0}$, so the
oscillator condition is not an additional admissibility condition on this
model. Applying the idealization to a concrete medium requires a separate
model of its fluctuations.
No value of $c$, of $m$, or of $\mathbf g$ is asserted by this item, and using
measured values for them is an empirical premise with its own conditions and
uncertainty.

**(v) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes it;
it selects no law of nature on its own and proves nothing about the actual
motion of any body in any medium. Its consequences within the model are the
subject of the companion example on terminal-velocity approach.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $(t,z(t))\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $(t,z(t))\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Adopt the force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: time window
$I_{0}$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, and a force map $F$ continuous and locally Lipschitz in
the state variable, locally uniformly in time, on
$D=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$. Let
$\mathcal F(t,x,v)=\bigl(v,\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\bigr)$ be the associated
first-order field and let motions and maximal motions be as in
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Fix an initial datum
$(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})\in I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ and write
$z_{0}=(x_{0},v_{0})$.

1. **Local existence.** There is $h>0$ and there is a motion $x$ of the model
   on $[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$ and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$;
   moreover such a motion is exactly one of class $C^{2}$ satisfying
   $m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}(t,x(t),\dot x(t))$ for all $i$ and all
   $t\in[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]$.
2. **Uniqueness.** If $x:J\to Q$ and $\tilde x:\tilde J\to Q$ are motions of
   the model with the same initial datum,
   $x(t_{0})=\tilde x(t_{0})=x_{0}$ and $\dot x(t_{0})=\dot{\tilde x}(t_{0})=v_{0}$,
   then $x=\tilde x$ on $J\cap\tilde J$.
3. **Quantitative cylinder.** Let $h,r>0$ satisfy
   $C:=[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]\times\overline B(z_{0},r)\subseteq D$, put
   $M:=\sup\{\lVert\mathcal F(t,z)\rVert_{2}:(t,z)\in C\}$ and let $\Lambda$
   be a state-Lipschitz constant of $\mathcal F$ on $C$. If $hM\le r$ and
   $\Lambda h<1$, then there is exactly one motion on $[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]$
   through the datum whose state graph $(t,(x(t),\dot x(t)))$ lies in $C$, and
   every motion through the datum agrees with it on the intersection of its
   interval with $[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]$.
4. **Maximal motion.** There is exactly one maximal motion with the datum:
   its maximal interval $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing $t_{0}$ and
   contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the datum is its restriction.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force model: clause 1 locates a
solution only near $t_{0}$ and bounds no interval length in terms of the data,
clause 4 asserts no completeness of $J_{\max}$ in $I_{0}$, and no empirical
content is claimed.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k\in\mathbb R$ be given real numbers, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). The **damped driven oscillator model** with data $(m,c,k,f)$ is the second-order equation

$$m\,x''(t)+c\,x'(t)+k\,x(t)=f(t),\qquad t\in I .$$

A **solution** of the model on an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior is a twice differentiable $x:J\to\mathbb R$ such that the identity holds for every $t\in J$, derivatives being ordinary real derivatives ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The model is called **homogeneous** when $f\equiv 0$, **undamped** when $c=0$, and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

The **phase-plane equation** of the model has right-hand side

$$G_f:I\times\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad G_f(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{f(t)-c\,v-k\,x}{m}\Bigr).$$

Here $\mathbb R^2$ is the **phase plane**, with coordinates $(x,v)$, where $x$ is the **displacement** and $v$ the **velocity**. For an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior, a differentiable curve $z=(x,v):J\to\mathbb R^2$ solves the phase-plane equation when $z'(t)=G_f(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$, using the domain-relative derivative at any included endpoint ([[def-derivative]]). If $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$, then $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ solves this equation; conversely, if $t\mapsto(x(t),v(t))$ solves it, then $v=x'$ and $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$. When $J$ is open, this is the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] on the open domain $J\times\mathbb R^2$. For the homogeneous model the right-hand side is written $G_0(x,v)=(v,-(cv+kx)/m)$.

The **characteristic polynomial** of the model is

$$p(\lambda):=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k,$$

with **discriminant** $\Delta:=c^2-4mk$. When $k>0$ define the **undamped frequency** $\omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}$, the **damping rate** $\gamma:=c/(2m)$ and, when $4mk>c^2$, the **damped frequency** $\omega:=\sqrt{k/m-\gamma^2}=\sqrt{4mk-c^2}/(2m)$; the corresponding square roots are the nonnegative real ones.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, $k\ge0$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Fix $t_0\in I$ and data $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$. Let $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be the (unique) solution of the associated homogeneous model with time domain $\mathbb R$ and zero forcing, with $g(0)=0$ and $g'(0)=1/m$.

Then:

1. There is exactly one solution $x:I\to\mathbb R$ of the forced model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f$ with $x(t_0)=x_0$ and $x'(t_0)=v_0$. It is twice differentiable on $I$, with derivatives at included endpoints taken relative to $I$, and $x''$ is continuous on $I$ in its relative topology.
2. If $x_h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is any homogeneous solution with $x_h(t_0)=x_0$ and $x_h'(t_0)=v_0$ (it exists and is unique by [[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]] and [[prop-cm-oscillator-degenerate-and-repulsive-cases]]), then
$$x(t)=x_h(t)+\int_{t_0}^tg(t-s)f(s)\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, let $k\le0$, and consider the model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero. In the three cases below, $x:J\to\mathbb R$ runs over solutions on intervals $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior.

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Double zero root ($k=0$, $c=0$).** Then on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if $x(t)=A+Bt$ for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a unique global member of this family. For every datum $(x_0,v_0)$ there is a unique global solution on $\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$, $x'(0)=v_0$, namely $x(t)=x_0+v_0t$.
2. **Simple zero root ($k=0$, $c>0$).** Then on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if
$$x(t)=A+Be^{-ct/m}$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a unique global member of this family. For every datum $(x_0,v_0)$ there is a unique global solution on $\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$, $x'(0)=v_0$, namely the member with $A=x_0+\frac{m v_0}{c}$ and $B=-\frac{m v_0}{c}$. This global solution has limit $A$ as $t\to+\infty$; any local solution on an interval unbounded above has the same limit along that interval.
3. **One positive and one negative root ($k<0$).** Put $$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt{c^2-4mk}}{2m}.$$ Then $\lambda_-<0<\lambda_+$, both are real roots of the characteristic polynomial, and on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a global member of this family. In particular the global solution $t\mapsto e^{\lambda_+t}$ has data $x(0)=1$, $x'(0)=\lambda_+$ and satisfies $e^{\lambda_+t}\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$: the model has an unbounded solution growing exponentially on $[0,\infty)$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

Throughout, $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ are **abbreviations and not real numbers**,
exactly as in [[def-interval]] and [[def-divergence-to-infinity]]. Every phrase
below is a single abbreviation for a displayed condition on reals, and no
arithmetic is ever performed with the symbols.

**Limits at $+\infty$.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be **not bounded above**
([[def-bounded-set]]), let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. We
write

$$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$$

when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $M$ such that

$$|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for every } x \in A \text{ with } x > M .$$

**Limits at $-\infty$.** Let $A$ be **not bounded below**. We write
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L$ when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a
real $M$ with $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ for every $x \in A$ with $x < M$.

**Why unboundedness is required.** It plays exactly the role the limit-point
condition plays in [[def-function-limit]]. Saying that $A$ is not bounded above
says that no real is an upper bound of $A$, that is, that for every real $M$
there is $x \in A$ with $x > M$ ([[def-bounded-set]],
[[def-complete-ordered-field]]); so the set over which the condition quantifies
is never empty and the condition is never vacuous. Without the hypothesis every
real $L$ would satisfy it and the notation would not denote.

**Uniqueness, proved here.** Suppose $A$ is not bounded above and
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L'$ with
$L \ne L'$. Then $|L - L'| > 0$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), so
$\varepsilon := |L - L'|/2 > 0$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]],
[[lem-of-inverse-positive]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]]). Choose reals $M_1, M_2$
witnessing the two conditions at this $\varepsilon$ and let $M$ be the larger of
them, the order being total. Since $A$ is not bounded above there is $x \in A$
with $x > M$, hence with $x > M_1$ and $x > M_2$, and then

$$|L - L'| = |(L - f(x)) + (f(x) - L')| \le |f(x) - L| + |f(x) - L'| < 2\varepsilon = |L - L'|$$

([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[lem-of-add-order]]),
which trichotomy forbids. So $L = L'$, and the notation
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x)$ denotes a single real. The same four lines, with the
inequalities on $x$ reversed, give uniqueness at $-\infty$.

**Infinite limits at a point.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit
point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$. We write

$$f(x) \to +\infty \ \text{ as } \ x \to c$$

when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that $f(x) > M$ for
every $x \in A$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$; and $f(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to c$
when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ with $f(x) < M$ for every
such $x$.

**This library does not write $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = +\infty$.** The right-hand
side would not be an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and writing the equation would
silently move the discussion into the extended real line, a structure that is
not a field. That is the convention already fixed by
[[def-divergence-to-infinity]] for sequences and by [[rem-sup-conventions]] for
suprema, and it is kept here. In particular none of the rules of
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]] may be applied to a function tending to
$\pm\infty$.

**Combined forms.** Let $A$ be not bounded above and $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$. We
write $f(x) \to +\infty$ as $x \to +\infty$ when for every real $N$ there is a
real $M$ with $f(x) > N$ for every $x \in A$ with $x > M$. The other forms are
obtained the same way, by pairing one of the two conditions on $x$ (unbounded
above, unbounded below) with one of the two conditions on $f(x)$ (above every
real, below every real); each is again a single abbreviation for the displayed
condition, and none of them is an equation.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: The vector equation $m\ddot x=m\mathbf g-c\dot x$ is, in the frame's coordinates, the three scalar equations $m\ddot x_{j}=m g_{j}-c\dot x_{j}$ for $j=1,2,3$, each the scalar model of [L2] with $k=0$, $c>0$ and constant forcing $f_{0}=mg_{j}$; in particular each scalar initial value problem has exactly one solution on $\mathbb R$ by [L2].

Candidate and its derivatives: set $v_{\infty}=(m/c)\mathbf g$ and $$\xi_{j}(t):=x_{0,j}+v_{\infty,j}t+\frac{m}{c}\bigl(v_{0,j}-v_{\infty,j}\bigr)\bigl(1-e^{-ct/m}\bigr);$$ then by [L3] $\xi_{j}'(t)=v_{\infty,j}+(v_{0,j}-v_{\infty,j})e^{-ct/m}$ and $\xi_{j}''(t)=-\frac{c}{m}(v_{0,j}-v_{\infty,j})e^{-ct/m}$, so $$m\xi_{j}''+c\xi_{j}'=-c(v_{0,j}-v_{\infty,j})e^{-ct/m}+c v_{\infty,j}+c(v_{0,j}-v_{\infty,j})e^{-ct/m}=cv_{\infty,j}=mg_{j},$$ the scalar equation of step 1.1; moreover $\xi_{j}(0)=x_{0,j}$ and $\xi_{j}'(0)=v_{\infty,j}+(v_{0,j}-v_{\infty,j})=v_{0,j}$.

By uniqueness in [L2] each $\xi_{j}$ is the unique scalar solution on $\mathbb R$ with the datum, so the vector curve $x(t):=(\xi_{1}(t),\xi_{2}(t),\xi_{3}(t))$ displayed in the Example satisfies the vector equation for all $t\in\mathbb R$ with values in $Q=\mathbb R^{3}$ and the stated datum; by [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]] clause (c) it is a motion of the model, and it is defined on all of the time window. By [[pthm-cm02-ivp]] clauses 2 and 4 every motion with the same datum is the restriction of this one, so it is the unique maximal motion, with maximal interval $\mathbb R$; this proves claim 1.

Velocity and approach to the terminal velocity: from step 2.1, $\dot x(t)-v_{\infty}=(v_{0}-v_{\infty})e^{-ct/m}$, so by [L4] $\lvert\dot x(t)-v_{\infty}\rvert_{2}=\lvert v_{0}-v_{\infty}\rvert_{2}\,e^{-ct/m}$ for every $t$. The factor decays to $0$: given $\varepsilon>0$, for $t>\frac{m}{c}\cdot\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$ one has $\frac{ct}{m}>\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$ and hence, using $\exp(s)\ge1+s$ at $s=\frac{ct}{m}>0$, the reciprocal comparison of [L3] and $\frac{m}{ct}<\varepsilon$, $$0<e^{-ct/m}=\frac{1}{e^{ct/m}}\le\frac{1}{1+ct/m}<\frac{m}{ct}<\varepsilon.$$ Therefore $\lvert\dot x(t)-v_{\infty}\rvert_{2}\le\lvert v_{0}-v_{\infty}\rvert_{2}\,e^{-ct/m}\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$, i.e. $\dot x(t)\to v_{\infty}$ ([[def-limits-at-infinity]]); this proves claim 2.
