Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

derivations.claim: Force from the potential: fix $x\neq0$ and a coordinate index $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, and let $e_i$ be the corresponding standard coordinate vector. For $|h|<|x|/2$, [L3] gives $|x+he_i|\ge|x|-|h|>0$, so the difference quotient is defined; also $|x+he_i|\to|x|>0$. Rationalizing the difference of squares gives $\frac{|x+he_i|-|x|}{h}=\frac{2x_i+h}{|x+he_i|+|x|}\to\frac{x_i}{|x|}$. Therefore $$\partial_iU(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{-k/|x+he_i|+k/|x|}{h}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{k(|x+he_i|-|x|)}{h|x+he_i||x|}=\frac{kx_i}{|x|^{3}}.$$ By the definition of the Euclidean gradient in [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (iii), $-\nabla U(x)=-k\,x/|x|^{3}$; this is the model's force map, continuous and locally Lipschitz on $Q$ by [L1] and [[ex-cm02-force-model-regularity-checks]]. Its dimension is $[k]/[x]^2=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, as required by [L5].

Set $\kappa:=k/m>0$, let $r_{0}>0$ have dimension $\ell$, and define
$$T:=\frac{\sqrt{2}\,r_{0}^{3/2}}{3\sqrt{\kappa}},\qquad v_{0}:=-\sqrt{\frac{2\kappa}{r_{0}}}.$$
Then $[T]=\tau$ and $[v_0]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ by [L5], and the definitions give $T^{2}=2r_{0}^{3}/(9\kappa)$ and $2r_{0}/(3T)=\sqrt{2\kappa/r_{0}}=-v_{0}$. Take the initial datum $x(0)=r_{0}e_{1}$, $\dot x(0)=v_{0}e_{1}$.

For $t<T$ put $s(t):=1-t/T>0$, let $q(t)$ be the unique positive cube root of $s(t)^{2}$, and set $r(t):=r_{0}q(t)$ and $x(t):=r(t)e_{1}$. This defines $q$ by [L6]. The cube-root map is continuous on $[0,\infty)$: for nonnegative $a,b$, if $\alpha^{3}=a$ and $\beta^{3}=b$, then $|\alpha-\beta|^{3}\le|a-b|$, since $\alpha^{2}+\alpha\beta+\beta^{2}\ge(\alpha-\beta)^{2}$; applying this to $a=s(t+h)^{2}$ and $b=s(t)^{2}$ gives $q(t+h)\to q(t)$. For $h\to0$ with $t+h<T$, rationalizing and using $s(t+h)=s(t)-h/T$ gives $$\frac{q(t+h)-q(t)}{h}=\frac{(s(t+h)^{2}-s(t)^{2})/h}{q(t+h)^{2}+q(t+h)q(t)+q(t)^{2}}\longrightarrow-\frac{2s(t)}{3Tq(t)^{2}},$$ so $q'(t)=-2s(t)/(3Tq(t)^{2})$. Differentiating this identity by [L2] and using $s'=-1/T$ and $q^{3}=s^{2}$ gives $q''(t)=-2/(9T^{2}q(t)^{2})$. Thus $x$ is $C^{2}$ on $(-\infty,T)$ and $$\dot r(t)=-\frac{2r_{0}s(t)}{3Tq(t)^{2}},\qquad \ddot r(t)=-\frac{2r_{0}}{9T^{2}q(t)^{2}}.$$ Moreover $q(t)\to0$ as $t\uparrow T$: for each $\varepsilon>0$, $q(t)\ge\varepsilon$ would imply $s(t)^{2}=q(t)^{3}\ge\varepsilon^{3}$, contradicting $s(t)^{2}\to0$ once $t$ is sufficiently close to $T$.

The equation holds: from $T^{2}=2r_{0}^{3}/(9\kappa)$ one has $2r_{0}/(9T^{2})=\kappa/r_{0}^{2}$, so step 1.3 gives $\ddot r(t)=-\kappa/(r_{0}^{2}q(t)^{2})=-\kappa/r(t)^{2}$. Hence $\ddot x(t)=-\kappa e_{1}/r(t)^{2}=-k e_{1}/(m r(t)^{2})$ and $F(x(t))=-k r(t)e_{1}/r(t)^{3}=-k e_{1}/r(t)^{2}$, so $m\ddot x(t)=F(x(t))$ for every $t<T$. Also $q(0)=1$, $q'(0)=-2/(3T)$, and step 1.2 gives $x(0)=r_{0}e_{1}$ and $\dot x(0)=-(2r_{0}/(3T))e_{1}=v_{0}e_{1}$. Since $q(t)>0$ for $t<T$, $x(t)\in Q$ and $t\in I_{0}=\mathbb R$ throughout; by [L1], $x$ is a motion through the datum on $(-\infty,T)$.

No extension past $T$: suppose a motion $\tilde x$ with the same datum were defined on an interval containing some $t_{*}>T$. By the uniqueness clause of [L1] it agrees with $x$ on the intersection of their intervals; that intersection contains $[0,T)$ because the interval of $\tilde x$ contains both $0$ and $t_{*}$. It is continuous at $T$, and step 1.3 gives $q(t)\to0$ as $t\uparrow T$, so $\tilde x(T)=\lim_{t\uparrow T}x(t)=0$. But a motion's values must lie in $Q=\mathbb R^{3}\setminus\{0\}$ at every time of its interval, a contradiction. Thus no motion through the datum extends past $T$, and by the maximality clause of [L1] the maximal motion is $x$ on $(-\infty,T)$, with finite right endpoint $b=T$.

Escape consistent with the breakdown criterion: as $t\uparrow T$, $q(t)\to0$ while $|\dot r(t)|=2r_{0}s(t)/(3Tq(t)^{2})\to+\infty$, since $\bigl(s(t)/q(t)^{2}\bigr)^{2}=1/q(t)\to+\infty$ and the quotient is positive. Thus the state $(x(t),\dot x(t))$ leaves every compact subset of $U=Q\times\mathbb R^{3}$ near $T$ in both ways predicted by [[pthm-cm02-continuation]] clause 4: its velocity is unbounded and its position approaches the excluded configuration. The refuted all-time-existence statement is false for this model.
